subtitle: Announcement of a working group meeting to discuss network I/O and interactive graphics

tldr.problem: Early network researchers needed to discuss how to provide flexible I/O and interactive graphics capabilities for network users.
tldr.mechanism: An RFC announces a meeting at MIT Lincoln Laboratory on May 8, 1970, to present the Local Interaction Language (LIL) for the Terminal Support Processor (TSP) system.
tldr.outcome: The meeting brought together interested researchers to discuss practical challenges of running interactive programs over the early ARPANET.

today: This working group meeting was part of early discussions about network services and interactive applications. Modern networks support rich interactive experiences, but the problems discussed—I/O design, interactive graphics, and user input over networks—remained central challenges for decades.

sections.title: Meeting Proposal
sections.content:
The RFC announces a meeting at MIT Lincoln Laboratory on Friday, May 8, 1970, at 9:30 AM. The purpose is to present the Local Interaction Language (LIL), a system designed to provide flexible I/O capabilities for network users.

Each participating host site is invited to send as many or as few interested individuals as they wish. The meeting is framed as a working group session rather than a formal conference.
sections.plainLanguage: A meeting is planned to talk about making the network work better for programs that draw pictures and take user input.

sections.title: The TSP System and LIL
sections.content:
The Terminal Support Processor (TSP) system aims to provide maximum flexibility in how network users can input and output data. To achieve this flexibility, TSP is user-programmable in an interpretable language called LIL (Local Interaction Language).

LIL has primitives specifically designed for two tasks: manipulating tree structures for interactive graphics, and handling message-oriented input/output. The language combines these capabilities with general-purpose programming constructs to let users specify both the I/O handlers and the display structures their application needs.
sections.plainLanguage: LIL is a language that lets you program how the network program talks to you, with special tools for drawing and receiving user input.

sections.title: Interactive Programs Over the Network
sections.content:
A key discussion topic at the meeting will be the challenges of running interactive programs over the ARPA network. Interactive graphics and real-time user input present different constraints than batch data transfer.

Interested parties should contact A. G. Nemeth or J. Forgie at MIT Lincoln Laboratory (contact info provided in the RFC). A working document on LIL was to be mailed about a week before the meeting to interested individuals.
sections.plainLanguage: When programs let people draw and click things, the network has to be fast enough. This meeting will talk about how to make that work.
